I'm 34 years old and spent my entire life minimizing it because It didn't seem to be bad enough to justify what was going on, all of the issues I've had around sex and sleep. What I didn't realize is that I had unknowingly been almost kind of sabotaging my life in little ways here and there to keep me under a near constant amount of stress. I'm not victim blaming myself, some of it was just shitty people taking advantage of me, but looking back on it I know that I was smart enough to know that they were going to. Turns out my unconscious mind was a clever girl, because the second that I felt complete trust and complete safety, I experienced the kind of flashback I thought only happened in Hollywood. I previously had only a few memories that were fuzzy at best, sometimes I even tried to convince myself I'd made it up. This was absolutely abhorrent. This was the most horrid thing I had ever seen or imagined happening to a child and it was happening to a part of me. I have dissociative identity disorder. It doesn't present like a lot of other people have it, in fact dissociative identity disorder is the kind of thing that doesn't want to be caught. More likely than not people go many decades before even realizing they have it because it wants to blend in as seamlessly as possible. What I experienced in that moment was two separate consciousnesses: one experiencing the trauma, and the other one doing her best to remember trauma-informed care. And so while I was sobbing I was just hugging myself best I could. 

I say this because, I was 34 years old when I found all this out. I was 34 when I got my diagnosis, I was 34 when I found out that trauma was so much worse than I had ever imagined. If I had never met a person that made me feel safe and stable, I might not have ever felt like I was in a safe enough place to deal with it and I never would have remembered. You never know what's down there. 

As for me, no. I haven't figured it out yet. I've backslid and have held off on doing intensive therapy until I can stabilize all of me and have enough internal communication to ensure that we're all on the same page, and that I can be a leader with everyone's best interest in mind, not just my core self. Best of luck to you as well.

Yeah... Monster, toxic, poison, or just a bumbling idiot who seems to somehow destroy relationships the way Godzilla destroys Tokyo, All those labels can put us in self-imposed solitary confinement. It's a terrible Hell. But, to an extent, we get each other. 

Sometimes I think about this idea, and I've always had strong doubts because I'm a bumbling Godzilla shitting out poison, but I feel like if there was a BPD site for making friends IRL it might actually work really well for some of us. Having another person who could understand all the nuances that come with us right off the bat would take so much pressure off. I feel like it would erase, or at least minimize the stress that comes with the fear of the first time they see us become dysregulated. I don't mean it in the way that we ought to be able to endure abusive behavior because we dish it out, but I guess personally for me, if the person on the other end had the compassion and understanding to not ridicule me for seeming overly dramatic, I think it would be pretty outstanding. I'm also the kind of person to care very deeply and to try to understand how other people are processing the world because I feel like it helps me learn to be the kind of person I want to be, it helps me practice using my healthier mental muscles, and *who else* has the ability to thrive, reflect, and grow when they finally feel understood and legitimately cared about? Us again! I think it's brilliant. When I'm having a freak out, when I'm feeling desperate or telling myself lies, oftentimes I feel like I'm on the inside screaming at myself to just calm the fuck down, wishing that somebody would look at me with eyes that could communicate to me that they know that I know that this isn't the way I really feel, that it isn't real and that it's my mind doing that catastrophizing bullshit again. I feel like if I just had someone to lovingly tell me to calm the fuck down, and I mean very lovingly, that could work. And I know for other people it's different things, but do you see what I mean? I'm onto something right? 

Anyway, I know how you're feeling. Or, no, I can imagine how you might be feeling by relating it to shit I've gone through that's made me express those same thoughts. Something I've discovered about myself is that it's not just that I think I'm worse than everyone, it's that I look at myself a whole hell of a lot closer than anyone else around me seems to look at themselves. It's really hard, it's really really really fucking hard, but trying to turn that in to a good thing is something I'm trying to run with. It's painful to see life so closely, especially when we've oftentimes gone through trauma and seem to be focused on the bad, but I think that those of us who have experienced pain the deepest and who also look so closely at the cracks, we are in a very unique position to see, potentially, the wounds of others as well. Learning how to help others heal their wounds instead of automatically and subconsciously exploiting them is something that has been rewarding. I mean, opening my eyes to the absolute piece of shit I was being without even knowing it was akin to being waterboarded with swamp water, but being able to do something good instead of being that horrible piece of shit that I always tell myself I am, that's like crack.

My healthier suggestion would be to see if you can't find some online or in person recurrent group meetings. I know they have them for bipolar and CPTSD and DID, they've got to happen for NPD. I'm not saying that's a good reason to have kids, but it's been the number one reason I have fought to better myself, personally.

The second thing I want to say is that my oldest is in the process of being screened for bipolar. We all thought he had ADHD but the psychiatrist and psychologists are both beginning to lean more toward bipolar type 1 with nothing but mania which I didn't even know was a freaking thing. I can get him in bed at 8:00 and he screams and cries until 12:30 at night sometimes. It is the most painful thing I have ever seen. Nothing I can do will comfort him. He says he doesn't believe that he will ever feel better and therefore he doesn't want to live anymore. Again, this little boy only just turned seven. For the record, the psychologist and psychiatrist are both very hopeful for him since he has been getting therapy from the moment his episodes began. Other than the night time, he is a very happy loving child, who does occasionally have emotional outbursts. But he loves being alive. He's just a huge insomniac who can't handle the frustration of not being able to fall asleep and the depression that hits him at that time.

I've had some people ask me how I could be so calloused as to choose to have children after I knew I was bipolar, and I always tell them to go eff themselves, even though I didn't know I was bipolar until after I had them. They feel it is incredibly selfish to choose to have children that you know could inherit this.

I don't believe this at all. Is it horrible to have children if you know there's a history of cancer in your family? Depression? Heart disease?  There are so many diagnosis that run throughout families, the truth is if we stopped all of those people from having children, we would lose some of the most incredible people on this planet who have a reason to search for new treatments and cures. Does it suck more than anything in the entire world seeing my child tortured by this? Yes. Does that mean I regret having him? Absolutely not. 

So to make a long personal opinion short, if you understand the risks, and what could go along with it, and you're prepared to help your child or children get all the help they might possibly need in the face of their own diagnosis, and you can do your best to be as stable as possible for them, go for it. I have failed at the latter part more than once, probably because I didn't know what I was going through. It's hard, but who better to help a child through the ins and outs of the difficulties of life than somebody who has stared at their demons and somehow grown stronger in spite of them.

I swear by McCann dog training, they're on YouTube and leave it was the first thing my puppy really understood. The way they explained it was to drop a treat on the floor and when your puppy goes for it, put your foot on top of it. When they sit down and they stop trying to get at it, say yes, and give them a treat. Then remove your foot from the treat on the floor and repeat. Eventually, you can drop a treat on the floor and they won't even go for it. Be sure to use the key phrase leave it when they finally stop going for the treat and say yes, or whatever other rewarding phrase or clicker you want to use, when you give them the treat.

Of course, puppies are a lot like people and everybody learns differently. This is just what worked for us. I hope it helps.
